read: full: abstract, sections 1-6 and the impact statement (pp. 1-10), Appendix A, A.1, A.2, A.4, A.5, A.6 and A.7 (pp. 13-17, 24-27); skimmed the model-response examples A.3 (pp. 18-23) and the references
venue_now: ICML 2025: 'Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025' (p1 footer); the file is arXiv:2508.08292v2 of 27 Aug 2025 (p1). The May entry cites an earlier version at the 4th MATH-AI Workshop at NeurIPS'24.
what_it_is: Putnam-AXIOM is a benchmark of 522 problems from the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition (1938-2023), chosen or modified to have a single final answer that can be checked automatically; 221 of them (42.3%) went through 'modified boxing', a trivial extra step added so that a proof or multi-answer problem ends in one boxed answer (pp. 1, 4). A companion Variation set gives 100 of the problems (19.2%) Python scripts that rename variables and, for 37 of them, also change constants (which changes the step-by-step solution and the answer), with rephrased statements; each script can produce unlimited new instances, and evaluation uses five random snapshots (pp. 4-5). Answers are graded by a SymPy equivalence check on the boxed answer (pp. 2, 5, 26). The paper also proposes Teacher-Forced Accuracy (TFA), the share of tokens of the reference solution that a model predicts correctly when conditioned on the gold prefix, as a cheap proxy for reasoning quality (pp. 5-6). o1-preview scores 41.94% on the originals, and 18 of 21 models score lower on the varied problems than on the matching originals (Table 1 p7; Table 2 p14, counted).
domain: university-level competition mathematics (Putnam), in 11 domains: geometry, algebra, trigonometry, calculus, linear algebra, combinatorics, probability, number theory, complex numbers, differential equations and analysis (p4)
size: 522 original problems, 221 with modified boxing, and 100 functional variations (37 constant-and-variable, 63 variable-only) (p4); 18 models on the originals (Table 1, p7) and 21 in the variation comparison (Table 2, p14); TFA validated on MATH with 15 open models (p8)
source_of_items: competitions (Putnam exams 1938-2023 with their official solutions, p4, p13), 221 modified to end in a single boxed answer (p4); the variations are perturbed from these by per-problem Python scripts (pp. 4-5)
instances: static (the 522 originals) plus perturbed (the Variation set: per-problem scripts generate unlimited new instances for 100 problems; five random snapshots are evaluated; pp. 4-5)
has_gold_traces: yes: every problem keeps a fully written reference solution with the boxed answer moved to the end (pp. 3-4, 13; only the first official solution is kept, p13); constant changes also update the step-by-step solution (p4). The reference solutions feed TFA; they are not used to check the model's own steps.
evaluation: final answer: the boxed answer is compared with the ground truth by a SymPy equivalence function (normalise, parse_latex, simplify the difference to zero; pp. 2, 26), run through LM Harness (p5). Plus Teacher-Forced Accuracy, a likelihood-based proxy computed on the gold solution, which needs log-probabilities and is reported for open models only (pp. 6-7, 9). TFA does not score the model's own generated steps; there is no step-level verification of model output.
human_validation: None reported for the problems, the modified boxing or the variations. TFA is validated only by its correlation with boxed accuracy: 0.66 +/- 0.02 on average across MATH subsets with 15 open models (pp. 8-9; Table 5, p17) and 0.52 on Putnam-AXIOM, 0.62 without two outliers (Figure 4, p9); its correlation with expert grading of proofs is listed as future work (p9). The error analysis of model responses is a qualitative reading by the authors (pp. 7-8, 18-23).
contamination_measures: perturbations: functional variations (variable and constant changes, rephrasing) that generate unseen instances (pp. 1, 4-5); a LoRA fine-tuning experiment simulating contamination raised accuracy on the originals from 23% to 80% but on the variations only from 12% to 33% (p5). Data and code are public (p1).

engtrace_use.sentence: In mathematics, benchmarks ranging from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) to HardMath (Fan et al., 2024), Putnam-Axiom (Gulati et al., 2024), and GSM-Symbolic (Mirzadeh et al., 2024) rigorously test abstract logical deduction and reasoning stability. (S-M1)
engtrace_use.explanation: The gist fits Putnam-AXIOM: it is a hard, university-level competition benchmark (p4), and its Variation set tests whether accuracy survives changed variables and constants (pp. 4-5), which 'reasoning stability' loosely renders. But 'rigorously test abstract logical deduction' overstates what it measures: it scores only the final boxed answer (pp. 2, 5, 26), it turned 221 proof-style or multi-answer problems into single-answer ones (p4), and the authors show that answers reached through unjustified claims still count as correct (p7; Figures 5-6, pp. 18-19). The sentence also leaves out the two features that bear on EngTrace's own claims: programmatic functional variation as a defence against contamination (pp. 1, 4-5), a precedent for EngTrace's templates alongside GSM-Symbolic, and a proxy for reasoning computed on gold solutions (TFA, pp. 5-6). The May entry cites the 2024 workshop version; the text reviewed is the ICML 2025 version (p1), and the numbers below come from it.

suggested_wording: Putnam-AXIOM (Gulati et al., 2025) draws 522 problems from the Putnam competition, scores the final boxed answer by symbolic equivalence, and adds functional variations for 100 of them, scripts that change variable names and constants to produce unseen instances, on which most models score lower than on the originals.
facts_to_cite: 522 problems from the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition, 1938-2023, across 11 mathematical domains (p4).
221 problems (42.3%) were modified ('modified boxing') with an added final step so that each has a single boxed answer (p4).

Functional variations exist for 100 problems (19.2%): Python scripts that change variable names (63) or variables and constants (37) and rephrase the statement; each can generate unlimited new instances, and evaluation averages five random snapshots (pp. 4-5).
Grading compares the boxed final answer with the ground truth by a SymPy-based equivalence check (pp. 2, 26).
On the 522 originals o1-preview scores 41.94% (219/522), GPT-4o 19.35% and Claude 3.5 Sonnet 15.96% (Table 1, p7).
On the 100 varied problems, 18 of 21 models score lower than on the matching originals, e.g. o1-preview 43% against 51% and GPT-4o 22% against 30% (Table 2, p14; the 18 of 21 is my count).
Simulated contamination by LoRA fine-tuning raised accuracy on the originals from 23% to 80% but on the variations only from 12% to 33% (p5).

Teacher-Forced Accuracy, the share of reference-solution tokens a model predicts correctly under teacher forcing, correlates with boxed accuracy at 0.66 +/- 0.02 on MATH (15 open models) and 0.52 on Putnam-AXIOM; it needs log-probabilities, and its agreement with human grading is left to future work (pp. 6, 8-9, 17).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: programmatic variation of problems to produce unseen instances against contamination (pp. 4-5), the mechanism EngTrace's templates generalise; a gold reference solution for every problem, updated by the constant-change scripts (pp. 4, 13); fully automatic, deterministic final-answer checking (p26); the stated aim of going beyond the final answer (TFA, pp. 5-6). Lacks: an engineering or physical context (it is competition mathematics); generated instances for most of the set (only 100 of 522 problems have variations, and 63 of those change only variable names, leaving the answer unchanged; p4); step-level evaluation of the model's own output (TFA scores the likelihood of the gold solution, not the model's steps; pp. 6-7); any human validation of items, variations or TFA (TFA against expert grading is future work, p9); and a private pool (data and code are public, p1).
notes: Version and citation: the May entry (L992-997) cites the NeurIPS'24 MATH-AI workshop version with seven authors; the reviewed file is arXiv:2508.08292v2 (27 Aug 2025), published at ICML 2025 (PMLR 267, p1), with eight authors (Elyas Obbad added) and a title ending 'in LLMs'. The revised reference should cite the ICML 2025 version, and the numbers should come from it. Internal inconsistencies in this version: the abstract says o1-preview's accuracy 'drops by 19.6% (46.8% relative decrease)' on the variations and that 'the remaining eighteen models show the same downward trend, ten of them with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals' (p1); section 4.1 says o1-preview drops 17%, GPT-4o 36% and DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-32B 37.5% (p7); Table 2 shows o1-preview 51% to 43%, GPT-4o 30% to 22%, DeepSeek-Distilled-Qwen-32B 33% to 24%, and three of 21 models with no drop (p14); its caption says 'mean accuracies over five trials' though every entry is an integer out of 100. Appendix A.4 speaks of 262 original and 60 variation questions and says most evaluations, such as Figure 3, use only non-binary questions (p24). The revised text should not quote the abstract's 19.6% or 46.8%. Verdict boundary: a reviewer reading 'reasoning stability' as a fair summary of the Variation set could call the sentence accurate; I hold 'imprecise' because the benchmark grades final answers only, which does not 'rigorously test' deduction.
